comments.text:
As someone with a background in Classics, this whole "culture war" outrage is just exhausting. Emily Wilson's translation of the Odyssey is viewed in academic circles as just as valid as any other translations. The university I got my BA from does an annual read-a-thon of the Odyssey, and they switched to using her translation, as the professors viewed it as a superior translation to the one they had previously used.  Ancient Greeks also would have interacted with black people, in fact, the mythical princess Andromeda, whose whole thing is that she was extremely beautiful, was from the kingdom of Aethiopia, which is derived from a Greek compound word which translates to burnt-face or red-brown, and is where modern Ethiopia gets its name. Lupita Nyong'o being cast as a someone who is supposed to be extremely beautiful would not have been odd to an ancient Greek. Well, actually it would have been weird for an ancient Greek to be seeing a dramatic performance that included women, as they did not allow women to act. So unless Matt Walsh is okay with all of the female characters being depicted by cross-dressing men, we are going to have to accept that the movie is different from what the ancient Greeks would have been used to.

The stories of the Iliad and the Odyssey have been long adapted to fit into the society that was telling them, especially since they were passed along through oral traditions. Nolan making changes to the story to reflect modern society is just a continuation of that long tradition.

comments.text:
Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey may use the line “defying the gods” as a powerful piece of marketing, but it does not really reflect Homer’s Odysseus. Odysseus was not a modern-style rebel fighting against the gods. With the obvious exception of Poseidon, most of the gods were sympathetic to him, above all Athena, who repeatedly protects, guides, and helps him return home.

Odysseus himself also respects the gods. He prays to them, understands their power, and lives in a world where divine will shapes every human fate. His conflict with Poseidon is real, of course, especially after blinding Polyphemus and then foolishly revealing his name. But that is very different from “defying the gods” as a whole.

If Nolan has reduced the role of the gods or turned Odysseus into a man standing against them, that is more than a minor change. It reverses one of the central ideas of Homer’s poem. The original Odysseus is not defined by defiance of the divine, but by endurance, intelligence, reverence, and Athena’s protection. Nolan is free to make his own interpretation, but it should be seen as a modern reimagining, not as Homer’s Odyssey.
